title: The Essentials — Nintendo's Own Adventures
blurb: The console-sellers. Every one of these was built in-house by Nintendo (or its closest partners) to prove what the little indigo cube could do, and most still define their series today.
games: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker
Cel-shaded ocean epic that traded Hyrule Field for open water and proved a stylistic gamble could still be a masterpiece.
The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess
The darker, dungeon-dense Zelda closing out the GameCube era — best played in this version's original, un-mirrored control scheme.
The Legend of Zelda: Four Swords Adventures

A frantic four-player co-op Zelda that turns puzzle dungeons into a scramble of shoving, item-sharing chaos. Europe didn't see it until seven months later — Nintendo deliberately held the localization back so it wouldn't collide with another Zelda release that same holiday season.

Retro reinvented Samus in first-person without losing an ounce of Metroid's isolation — still the gold standard for the jump to 3D. The European release, which followed four months later, quietly changed more than the calendar: tougher enemies, several patched-out sequence breaks, extra narration, and a proper on-boot choice between 50Hz and 60Hz that spared PAL players the slowdown other conversions suffered.

A bleaker, harder sequel built around light and dark dimensions of one planet, rewarding patience with the series' best atmosphere. An unusual case for the era: the European release dropped 50Hz altogether and shipped 60Hz-only, rather than offering it as an optional toggle.
FLUDD-powered platforming on a sun-drenched island resort — Mario's most experimental 3D outing, equal parts beloved and divisive.

A launch-window showcase built entirely around vacuuming ghosts out of a haunted house — funnier and spookier than a spin-off had any right to be. The European and Australian release, five months later, added an entire bonus Hidden Mansion mode: a mirrored map with harder bosses and tougher ghost captures that North America never got.
Two racers per kart, swapping items on the fly — the series' most chaotic, most-missed multiplayer format.
Still argued over two decades later as the fastest, most technically deep entry in the series, and a fixture of competitive play.
A stranded astronaut commands an army of plant-creatures against a 30-day clock — real-time strategy shrunk down to a back garden.
Drops the timer and doubles the ideas, adding a second species and genuinely creepy cave-crawling to Nintendo's tiniest strategy series.

A cartridge that runs on the real calendar — debt, decorating, and small talk with animal neighbors, decades before 'cozy games' had a name. Europe's wait for it was the longest of any game on this list: two full years after the North American release, and a year behind even Australia's own delayed launch.

Turn-based RPG combat crossed with theatrical, fourth-wall-winking writing that's still held up as the series' comic high point. A curious localization footnote: the multi-language European disc removed the English text's hints that party member Vivian is transgender, and German did the same — but the French, Spanish, and Italian text sitting on that identical PAL disc kept it intact.

Blisteringly fast anti-gravity racing built with Sega's arcade team — punishing, gorgeous, and one of the best 60fps racers ever made. Its N64 predecessor was notorious for PAL slowdown; this one fixed it outright, with a proper 60Hz mode that ran European copies exactly as fast as the rest of the world's.

title: Third-Party Landmarks
blurb: Games that didn't come from Nintendo but still defined what GameCube ownership felt like — several of them changed their entire genre far beyond this one console.
games: Reworked the entire survival-horror genre around an over-the-shoulder camera and set-piece pacing — almost every third-person action game since owes it something.
A ground-up rebuild of the original mansion, with pre-rendered backgrounds still cited as some of the best-looking environments on the system.
A Lovecraftian horror unique to GameCube that fakes save-file corruption and volume changes as your character's sanity fails.
Michel Ancel's photojournalist-adventure flopped commercially and became one of the most beloved cult classics of the generation.
Star Wars Rogue Squadron II: Rogue Leader
A launch title that recreated the Death Star trench run so well it became the system's go-to graphical showpiece.
Star Wars Rogue Squadron III: Rebel Strike
Adds on-foot combat to the flight formula for a more uneven but still spectacular close to Factor 5's trilogy.
Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time
Time-rewind mechanics and acrobatic platforming that revived a dormant franchise and shaped a decade of action-adventure design.
Metal Gear Solid: The Twin Snakes
The PS1 classic rebuilt with MGS2's engine and cinematic new cutscenes — controversial among purists, gorgeous on GameCube.
Hideki Kamiya's cel-shaded, film-reel-powered brawler turns slow-mo and fast-forward into core combat tools.
A tighter, faster sequel with a second playable hero and even more inventive boss encounters.

title: RPGs & Long Adventures
blurb: GameCube's RPG shelf is smaller than its rivals', which makes it a great snapshot of the genre's mid-2000s range — card battlers, tactics games, and one very strange sky-pirate epic.
games: The series' console breakout, with real-time 'Linear Motion Battle' combat that made turn order feel like a brawler.
A Dreamcast favorite reborn with new content — airship exploration and a swashbuckling story still ranked among the genre's best.
Baten Kaitos: Eternal Wings and the Lost Ocean
A card-based battle system in a sky-world setting where the characters literally have no bodies below the shoulders.

A prequel refining the original's card combat into something faster and sharper — criminally overlooked as one of GameCube's last releases, and one Europe never got the chance to overlook at all: it never released there, Japan and North America only.
A GBA-linked, lantern-carrying co-op RPG that traded traditional Final Fantasy trappings for four-player couch adventuring.
The series' first console outing in the West — grid-strategy RPG combat whose permadeath tension still defines the genre.
Phantasy Star Online Episode I & II
Online action-RPG dungeon crawling, remarkable for offering broadband play on a Nintendo console years before that was standard.
Double battles and a noir-tinted Orre region — the first mainline-adjacent Pokémon RPG built for a home console.
A 'Shadow Pokémon' story that lets you purify corrupted creatures — the series' darkest home-console detour.
An unusual card-summoning RPG where the heroine never fights directly, only conjuring creatures pulled from a deck.

title: Fighting Games
blurb: Smash Bros. gets its own chapter above, so this one is the rest of the roster — from arcade-perfect 3D weapon duels to a crossover so strange it never left Japan.
games: Weapon-based 3D fighting at its most refined, with a GameCube-exclusive guest fighter in Link.
A deep crossover fighter with a beginner-friendly 'Easy Operation' mode layered over genuinely competitive systems.
Fighters who transform into beasts mid-combo — an overlooked series finding a natural home on GameCube.

Cel-shaded anime brawling that captures the show's ninja speed better than most licensed fighters manage. Nintendo published it in Europe two months later under a blunter title: simply Naruto: Clash of Ninja — European Version.
Story-mode battles built on a board-game overworld, bringing Z-Fighter spectacle to GameCube's smaller anime-fighter shelf.
A Smash-style crossover pitting Bomberman and Solid Snake against Optimus Prime — Japan-only, and every bit as odd as it sounds.
Adds weapon combat and Death Traps to the fatality-famous series, with a create-a-fighter mode unique to this generation.
Hip-hop-roster wrestling-brawler hybrid from the WWF No Mercy team, with an over-the-top story mode and soundtrack to match.

title: Shooters & Space Combat
blurb: First-person, third-person, top-down bullet hell — GameCube's shooter shelf punches well above its reputation, anchored by the ex-Rare team that built TimeSplitters.
games: A GoldenEye spiritual successor from ex-Rare staff, packed with a level editor and some of the deepest bot AI of its era.
Time-travel campaign structure and an even more generous Map Maker close out the trilogy on a high note.
A black-and-white polarity-switching bullet-hell shoot-'em-up that arcade purists still rank among the genre's absolute best.
Splits time between Arwing dogfights and on-foot combat — less beloved than its predecessors but home to some great set pieces.
A GoldenEye-flavored Bond shooter with tight split-screen multiplayer that filled the void before its own sequels arrived.
An FPS where you play a disembodied spirit possessing enemies, guards, and household objects to solve problems and fight back.
A dinosaur-hunting FPS prequel, rougher around the edges than its N64 predecessors but still a solid campaign shooter.
A World War II shooter that helped define the genre's console template, ported with a strong four-player split-screen suite.

title: Racing & Speed
blurb: Beyond Mario Kart and F-Zero (already in the essentials above), the racing shelf ranges from arcade-perfect risk-reward driving to a cel-shaded street racer that renders cars like a comic panel.
games: Arcade racing built entirely around risk — the faster and more recklessly you drive, the more boost you earn.
Sega's fare-hunting arcade classic ported almost note-for-note, thrash-punk soundtrack and all.
Jet-ski racing with water physics still held up as some of the most convincing in any racing game.
Snowboarding racing where the mountain itself is the obstacle — avalanche chases raise the stakes mid-run.
Masahiro Sakurai's stripped-down racer, where steering is automatic and drafting, charging, and open-world scavenging are the game.
Tuner-car customization and an open city map brought the street-racing boom to GameCube.
Futuristic anti-gravity bike racing in the Wipeout mold, fast and brutal with weapons thrown into the mix.

A cel-shaded street racer that renders cars like a moving comic book — unlike anything else on the system, at least in North America: a finished PAL GameCube version existed but was quietly cancelled, and Europe only ever got the game on PS2.

title: Sports
blurb: Nintendo's own sports spin-offs sit alongside the best of the era's arcade-sports boom — trick systems, Gamebreakers, and Mega Strikes over anything resembling a real rulebook.
games: Mushroom Kingdom courses and character-specific special shots make this the series' most purely fun entry. Europe waited eleven months for it, and the PAL disc — unusually for a first-party Mario sports title — never got a 60Hz option, staying locked to 50Hz throughout.
Gimmick courts and over-the-top Power Shots turn a straightforward tennis sim into pure Mario chaos.
Chemistry-based team-building and Star Swings give Mario's take on baseball real strategic depth.

Arcade soccer with no rules, illegal tackles, and Mega Strikes that can wipe out a goalkeeper entirely. Released in Europe about two weeks earlier than North America, and under a different name: Mario Smash Football.
Trick-heavy streetball with a Gamebreaker system, widely considered the high point of the whole Street series.
One continuous mountain instead of separate courses, turning snowboarding into a seamless, trick-chaining descent.
The series' peak, introducing the revert and online-style goals that shaped skateboarding games for a decade.
Fast three-on-three arcade soccer with Showtime moves and a personality-driven roster far removed from any real league.

title: Puzzle, Party & Rhythm
blurb: The couch-multiplayer heart of the console — rolling-ball mazes, board-game chaos, and two bongo drums that turned a curious rhythm spin-off into one of the system's best-remembered peripherals.
games: A launch-window arcade port that turns rolling a ball through a maze into one of the tightest, most replayable puzzle-platformers around.
More stages, more party-game modes — Bowling, Golf, Boat Race — refining an already-perfect formula.
The board-and-minigames formula at its most polished, before the series started leaning on gimmicks.
Swaps items for a capsule system and introduces Super Duel Mode, a full board built from minigame parts.
Hundreds of absurd five-second microgames compiled into a party game unlike anything else in Nintendo's library.

Rhythm game played on bongo peripherals, thumping and clapping along to a genuinely eclectic setlist — one that's genuinely different depending where you bought it, since music licensing meant Japan, North America, and Europe each got their own distinct regional tracklist.
A second helping of bongo rhythm action with a fresh tracklist and expanded four-player support — Europe's version swapped in its own regional song selection, same as the original game did.
A spinning-stick puzzle-action sequel that never made it West, prized by import collectors for its tight, tricky level design.

title: Strategy & Simulation
blurb: The console's smallest genre shelf is also its strangest — a god-game about raising mountains, a pinball-tactics hybrid, and a creature-evolution sim that has no real peer anywhere else.
games: Real-time strategy reimagined as direct squad-commanding action, closer to a cartoon war movie than a spreadsheet.
Build a fighting robot from swappable parts, then duel it out in arena battles with real build-crafting depth underneath. Never released in Europe — Japan and North America only.

Eat, evolve, and mutate your creature across generations — one of the strangest, most memorable simulation concepts ever shipped. Like Custom Robo, it stayed a Japan-and-North-America game; Europe never got an official release.

A god-game where you raise and lower an island's terrain to guide its tiny inhabitants, from the makers of SimTower. One of this collection's rare reversals: it released in Japan and Europe both in 2002, but never in North America at all.
Pinball crossed with real-time squad tactics and voice commands — one of the last and strangest games GameCube ever received.
An Animal Crossing-adjacent life-sim about paying off debt and helping townsfolk, never localized outside Japan.

title: Survival Horror
blurb: Beyond the two genre-defining Resident Evil entries already in earlier chapters, GameCube quietly built out a full horror shelf — vampires, psychics, and one relentless pursuer named Nemesis.
games: A prequel built around swapping between two characters in real time — one of the series' most puzzle-forward entries.
Jill Valentine hunted through Raccoon City by an unkillable pursuer that can show up almost anywhere.
The Dreamcast's fully-3D horror epic, expanded and polished for its GameCube release.
A psychic-powered stealth thriller overshadowed by its own studio's TimeSplitters games — worth revisiting for its telekinesis mechanics.
A half-vampire dhampir slices through Nazi occultists with blade and blood-drain powers, gleefully over the top.
Vampire revenge action steeped in the series' gothic mythology, action-first rather than puzzle-first.

title: Cult Classics, Curios & Japan-Only Gems
blurb: This is where a 'best of' list earns the word explorer. Suda51's fever dreams, a bongo-controlled platformer, a household robot cleaning a family's floors — the games that make the GameCube library genuinely one of a kind.
games: Suda51's rail-shooter fever dream, following seven personalities of one assassin through a story as confusing as it is unforgettable.
A stylish, balletic third-person shooter starring a laser-dodging heroine in a skintight suit — divisive on release, reassessed as ahead of its time.

A tiny household robot cleans up a family's problems (and floors), turning chores into one of GameCube's most quietly charming games. Europe didn't get its own release until nearly a year later, in 2006.
A short, punchy beat-'em-up platformer from the studio behind Gunstar Heroes, with Wario smashing everything in sight for cash.
Toy-robot collect-and-battle action that plays like a cross between Custom Robo and a tokusatsu cartoon — a cult favorite among import fans.
A platformer controlled entirely with bongo drums, clapping Donkey Kong through 16 fruit-strewn stages.
Originally a standalone Rare adventure retrofitted with Star Fox characters — plays like a Zelda-flavored detour for the series.
A remastered trio of Panel de Pon, Dr. Mario 64, and Yoshi's Cookie that never crossed the Pacific.

A top-down online RPG from the Mystery Dungeon studio, one of the system's rarer curiosities — and, like most of this chapter's imports, a Japan-only release with nothing resembling a Western version.
Turn-based strategy and robot-battling action in one Gundam-flavored package, unreleased outside Japan.

title: Licensed & Movie Tie-Ins Done Right
blurb: The genre most players write off entirely, closing the collection with proof that a licensed game could still be a genuinely great one on this console.
games: A GTA-style open-world romp through Springfield that's aged into a stone-cold classic in its own right.
LEGO Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy
The template for every LEGO game that followed, rebuilding Episodes IV-VI as slapstick, brick-based co-op.
The web-swinging physics that defined superhero open-world games for a decade, years before its own sequels caught up.
The Lord of the Rings: The Two Towers
A hack-and-slash retelling of the film's battles, gory and stylish enough to outclass most movie tie-ins of its day.
